planting.note: Plant rooted bulbils or basal offsets in spring in full sun and fast-draining, lean, rocky soil; established plants shrug off Mexican highland dry seasons and need almost no supplemental care.

directions: Furcraea longaeva is endemic to dry, rocky slopes and thorn-scrub habitats in the Mexican states of Guerrero, Oaxaca, and Puebla, where it grows as a solitary rosette of long, blue-green, sword-shaped leaves that arch upward much like a yucca. Give it full sun and sharply drained, mineral soil, and otherwise leave it alone; established plants tolerate long dry spells and resent soggy or heavy soils. After growing for a decade or more the rosette sends up an immense, fuzzy-stemmed flowering spike that can rival any inflorescence in the plant kingdom for size, attracting bees and other pollinators before the mother rosette dies; each spent flower can drop a tiny plantlet that roots readily, so gardeners usually propagate by collecting these bulbils or basal offsets rather than by seed.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Set out rooted basal offsets in spring in full sun and gritty, sharply drained soil; keep plants on the dry side, especially in winter, since cold-wet soil is more damaging to this species than cold alone.

directions: Furcraea parmentieri (long sold in nurseries under the synonym Furcraea bedinghausii) grows naturally on semi-arid mountain slopes of central and southern Mexico between roughly 8,000 and 10,000 feet, which gives it more cold tolerance than most of its lowland relatives. Over many years a stiff rosette of blue-gray, spine-edged leaves develops atop a slowly thickening, trunk-like stem, eventually producing a tall, branched, candelabra-like flower panicle packed with creamy yellow-green blooms that draw bees and hummingbirds. Site it in full sun with gritty, fast-draining soil and keep it dry through winter to prevent stem rot, since its high-elevation origin makes it prone to cold-wet damage rather than cold damage alone. New plants are best started from rooted basal offsets rather than seed.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

subcategory: Central American fiber and ornamental succulent

planting.note: Plant basal offsets in spring in full sun and lean, fast-draining soil; this species is rarely offered as seed, so division of pups is the practical route to new plants.

directions: Furcraea quicheensis is native to the pine-oak highlands and sandy basins of Chiapas, Mexico and adjacent Guatemala, where local growers have long stripped its slender, glaucous leaves for cordage and twine and have even planted it to stabilize drifting sand in the Guatemalan highlands. In cultivation the rosette of narrow, arching leaves gradually rises on a solitary, sometimes branching trunk, giving it a more elegant, agave-like silhouette than its bulkier cousins. It wants full sun and lean, fast-draining soil and is otherwise nearly maintenance-free, though it remains uncommon outside specialty succulent collections in the United States. Propagate by division of basal offsets, since flowering is infrequent and the species is rarely offered as seed.
sources: Huntington Botanical Gardens International Succulent Introductions (ISI)
